hypothesis: Among angiosperm species, the proportion with separate sexes (dioecious, plus monoecious as separate-sex flowers) is higher in woody species (trees) than in herbaceous species, in most plant families.
pass_criterion: Using the Dryad species-level file (SplistWithSexSyst.csv), the proportion of species with unisexual flowers (dioecy or monoecy) is higher in woody than in herbaceous species, with a two-sided Fisher or chi-square test at p<0.001 and an odds ratio of at least 1.5. In a family-level comparison, the woody proportion is higher in at least 60% of families that have at least 20 woody and 20 herbaceous species.
fail_criterion: The odds ratio for unisexual flowers (woody vs herbaceous) is below 1.1 or the difference is non-significant (p>=0.01), or the woody proportion is higher in fewer than 50% of the qualifying families.
interpretation: Darwin's 'trees' maps to the dataset's 'woody' growth form, which also includes shrubs and woody lianas; this is a coarser category than trees, and I note it as a limitation. Darwin's 'separate sexes' maps to dioecy (separate individuals), with monoecy (separate male and female flowers on one plant) tested as a second definition. His 'Orders' map to modern families. Darwin worked with the British flora, which is outside this dataset's scope, so the test is global. A secondary test excludes Australia to check Hooker's exception. The test uses species counts, not Darwin's count of British genera.

dataset.name: Global distribution and evolutionary transitions of angiosperm sexual systems
dataset.why_it_fits: It records sexual system (dioecy, monoecy, hermaphroditism) and growth form (woody vs herbaceous) for tens of thousands of angiosperm species. The files are GloSexSyst.csv, SplistWithSexSyst.csv, TransitionBetweenSexSyst.csv and a README. Exact column names must be read from the README, because the landing page does not list them.
